title: The prayer for neighbors
hook: a prayer asking to be generous and fair to the people next door
tomorrow: if you could ask for just one trait, which would it be?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer for parents: make me gentle to them. Today the same book of prayers steps out the front door and looks next door.
screen: `MAKE ME GENTLE TO THEM.` → `NOW, NEXT DOOR.`

segments.voice: The moving truck next door has blocked the driveway all morning. Someone's dad is shouting directions. A kid sits on a box, holding a cat carrier. On the neighborhood app, the first post is already up: whose truck is this? Long before apps, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told of an angel who kept raising one subject with him, over and over, until the Prophet began to wonder where it would end. The subject was the people next door. So where did it end?
screen: `A TRUCK IN THE DRIVEWAY.` → `AN ANGEL WHO KEPT ASKING.` → `WHERE DID IT END?`

segments.voice: It ended with family. In al-Bukhari and Muslim, the Prophet says Gabriel kept urging him about the neighbor until he thought the neighbor would be made an heir. An heir: written into the will, counted as kin. The Qur'an names two kinds, in Pickthall's words: “the neighbour who is of kin (unto you) and the neighbour who is not of kin.” Both are owed kindness. Later, the Prophet's great-grandson, Imam Ali Zayn al-Abidin, turned that urging into a prayer, kept in the Sahifa, his book of prayers. First he prays for his neighbors to be good to each other: gentle with their weak, visiting their sick, keeping each other's secrets, covering each other's faults. Then he turns to himself. Let me repay the ones who do wrong with good, he asks, think well of every one of them, be tender with the ones who are hurting, and give them what I give my own family. Notice what he doesn't ask. He never asks for nicer neighbors. He asks to become a better one. In this prayer the neighbor isn't a problem to manage. The neighbor is the reason to grow. A blocked driveway, a barking dog, a stranger holding a cat carrier: in this prayer, each one is a chance to become someone better.
screen: `GABRIEL KEPT URGING.` · `KIN OR NOT, BOTH ARE OWED.` · `THE SAHIFA PRAYS FOR THEM.` · `THEN: MAKE ME BETTER.` · then, large: `GOOD TO MY NEIGHBORS.`

segments.voice: Go door by door in your mind: left, right, across the street, upstairs, the desk beside yours. Name whoever is there, even if all you know is their dog. If you pray, you can hold each one up as you name them; if not, wish each of them one good thing.
The prayer for neighbors: in the Sahifa, a prayer for the neighbors' good, and to be good to them, even to the ones who do wrong.
For the road: good to my neighbors, including the ones I haven't met. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1639 COUNTS.` → `THE SAHIFA · 3 OF 4.` → `TOMORROW: ONE TRAIT. WHICH ONE?`

howItsDone: The Sahifa's prayers are read by Shia Muslims and by other Muslims too, alone or in gatherings; greeting new neighbors and bringing them food are customs Muslims tie to the hadith of Gabriel's urging.

match.prompt: who said what — tap the pairs.
pairs: thought the neighbor might become an heir
the neighbor of kin and not of kin

myth: the Qur'an asks kindness only for neighbors who are family
it names both: the neighbor who is of kin and the neighbor who is not.
Zayn al-Abidin asks to repay neighbors who do wrong with good
and to think well of every one of them.
the prayer mostly asks that the neighbors be kind to him
it prays for their good, and that he become a better neighbor.

fork.setup: the neighbor's tree drops leaves all over your yard every fall, and you've never spoken. what fits the prayer?
options: introduce yourself first; the leaves can wait for a friendly talk.
rake it quietly and never mention it; that's covering their fault.
ask them to trim the tree, since fairness has to run both ways.
fork.reveal: covering faults is in the prayer, but so is turning toward neighbors, greeting them, giving them what you'd give family. the prayer starts with the person, not the leaves.

original.note: Arabic: al-jar, the neighbor, the word in the hadith of Gabriel's urging and in the Qur'an.

trapdoor: what you thought: a neighbor is whoever happens to live next door.
what it means: someone so close the Prophet thought they'd inherit, owed kindness whether kin or not.
what a scholar hears: the hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim, Qur'an 4:36's two neighbors, and the Sahifa's prayer for neighbors and friends.
guess: a prayer asking to be generous and good to those next door
a blessing said when moving into a brand-new house
a group prayer held for a whole neighborhood

chat.says: new neighbors' truck blocked dad's car all morning. dadi's making samosas for them. do i HAVE to go?
options: Go. The angel kept urging the Prophet about neighbors. Samosas are a good start, truck or no truck.
Only if they apologize first. Being a good neighbor runs both ways, so wait for them.
Just don't bother them. Kindness to neighbors mostly means keeping a polite distance.
chat.meaning: The neighbor is owed kindness, kin or not, and Zayn al-Abidin asks to repay wrong with good. A blocked driveway doesn't cancel that.

Gabriel.meaning: the angel who brought revelation to the Prophet

Zayn al-Abidin.meaning: the Prophet's great-grandson, whose prayers fill the Sahifa

Sahifa.meaning: a book of Zayn al-Abidin's prayers

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6014; Sahih Muslim 2624 (Gabriel kept urging me about the neighbor)

sources.ref: Al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya 26 (his supplication for his neighbors and friends)

notes: Sahifa 26 paraphrased from memory of its structure: first asks that the neighbors act well toward each other (gentle with their weak, visiting their sick, keeping secrets, covering faults), then 'let me' repay their evildoers with good, think well of all, be tender with the afflicted, give them what I give my next of kin. The prayer is addressed to neighbors and friends 'who recognize our right'; the voice leaves that qualifier out. Confirm with a Shia Keeper.
Bukhari 6014 / Muslim 2624: 'until I thought he would make him an heir.' Paraphrased.
Pickthall 4:36 phrase; confirm wording and the parenthesis.
